stubs.angle: Asks what makes an HTTP API RESTful: resources identified by URLs, a uniform interface of standard methods, representations and stateless requests.
stubs.answerHinge: REST models nouns as resources addressed by URLs and manipulated through the standard HTTP methods, with each request carrying all the state the server needs.

stubs.angle: Asks how PUT and PATCH differ when updating a resource and what happens to fields the client omits.
stubs.answerHinge: PUT replaces the whole target representation with the one sent, while PATCH applies a set of partial changes described by the request body.

stubs.angle: Asks which response a POST that creates a new resource should return.
stubs.answerHinge: 201 Created with a Location header pointing at the new resource is the response RFC 9110 defines for successful creation.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select all HTTP methods that RFC 9110 defines as idempotent from a list including POST and PATCH.
stubs.answerHinge: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS are idempotent by definition, while POST and PATCH are not.

stubs.angle: Asks how a WebSocket connection is established and which status code the server returns on success.
stubs.answerHinge: The client sends an HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket and the server answers 101 Switching Protocols, after which the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames.

stubs.angle: A runnable snippet uses HttpClient with a stub HttpMessageHandler that prints the request URI; BaseAddress lacks a trailing slash, so the version segment is lost and the wrong URL is printed.
stubs.answerHinge: Relative URIs are resolved by RFC 3986 rules, so a BaseAddress without a trailing slash has its last segment replaced and a relative path with a leading slash replaces the whole path.

stubs.angle: Asks to compare versioning a web API through the URL path, a query string parameter and a header or media type, and when to pick each.
stubs.answerHinge: URL path versions are explicit and cache-friendly but change resource identity, while header or media type versions keep URLs stable at the cost of discoverability and tooling support.

stubs.angle: Asks why a browser application cannot call a standard gRPC service directly and what ASP.NET Core offers instead.
stubs.answerHinge: Browser APIs do not give the low-level control over HTTP/2 frames and trailers that gRPC needs, so browsers need gRPC-Web or a JSON transcoding endpoint.

stubs.angle: Asks how to make a POST that creates a payment safe for client retries after a timeout.
stubs.answerHinge: The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key and the server stores the key with the outcome, returning the stored result for a repeated key instead of executing the operation again.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select the error status codes with which the HTTP RFCs define the Retry-After header to tell the client when to try again, from a list including 400, 404, 409, 429 and 503.
stubs.answerHinge: Retry-After is defined for 503 Service Unavailable in RFC 9110 and for 429 Too Many Requests in RFC 6585, not for client errors such as 400, 404 or 409.

stubs.angle: Asks how to keep a long-lived static HttpClient from ignoring DNS changes without falling back to creating a client per request.
stubs.answerHinge: Setting SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime (available since .NET Core 2.1) recycles pooled connections so new ones resolve DNS again, which a singleton client otherwise never does.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select the transports ASP.NET Core SignalR can negotiate, from a list including gRPC streaming and raw TCP.
stubs.answerHinge: ASP.NET Core SignalR supports WebSockets, Server-Sent Events and Long Polling and falls back between them in that order.

stubs.angle: A non-runnable hub class keeps a per-user counter in an instance field and the reader must find the line that loses the state between calls.
stubs.answerHinge: Hub instances are transient and created for each hub method invocation, so state stored in hub fields does not survive and must live in a separate service or store.

stubs.angle: Asks how gRPC deadlines differ from a plain client timeout and how they should flow through a chain of service calls.
stubs.answerHinge: A deadline is sent to the server, which can observe it through the call cancellation token, and propagating it to downstream calls stops the whole chain from working past the moment the original caller gave up.

stubs.angle: After scaling a SignalR app from one to three instances behind a load balancer, some clients fail to connect and broadcasts reach only part of the users; the reader plans the diagnosis and fix.
stubs.answerHinge: Each server only knows its own connections, so scale-out needs sticky sessions for negotiation and fallback transports plus a backplane such as Redis or Azure SignalR Service to fan out messages.

stubs.angle: Asks how an HTTP API should expose an operation that takes minutes, without holding the request open.
stubs.answerHinge: The API returns 202 Accepted with a Location to a status resource that the client polls, and that resource reports progress and finally points to the result.

stubs.angle: A public API used by external partners needs a breaking change to a response contract; the reader decides how the team ships it without breaking clients.
stubs.answerHinge: Ship the change as a new version alongside the old one, announce a deprecation window with Deprecation and Sunset signals and usage monitoring, and retire the old version only when traffic and agreed dates allow.

stubs.angle: A platform with a public partner API and dozens of internal services must choose a request-response protocol for each side; the reader weighs REST and gRPC across years of evolution.
stubs.answerHinge: REST with JSON suits the public edge for reach, browser and tooling support, while gRPC suits internal calls for strict contracts, streaming and efficiency, at the cost of HTTP/2 requirements and weaker browser and proxy support.
